angle: Explaining the physics and engineering constraints that require the Falcon 9 first stage to use active propulsive descent rather than passive recovery systems.

beats.text: When a rocket falls back to Earth, gravity isn't enough to guide it home safely. Unlike a winged spaceplane, the Falcon 9 first stage cannot glide passively to its target, meaning it must use its engines to steer and slow down.

Early concepts used parachutes, but extreme atmospheric heating and high-velocity stress destroyed the boosters. Today, its restartable engines burn liquid oxygen and kerosene to actively fight physics.
Instead of drifting, the booster performs up to three controlled burns. During descent, grid fins steer the aerodynamic lift, while an entry burn slows the vehicle through the upper atmosphere.
Finally, carbon-fiber landing legs deploy. A final, precise engine firing provides a propulsive cushion, bringing the booster to a soft, controlled landing.

hook: Why does a falling rocket booster need to burn precious fuel just to land?
